Chapter 1: Chapter 1: The Day the Sun Died

6|
7|

![](chapter_images/ch01.png)

8|

The graph doesn't lie. Dr. Elena Vasquez has been staring at it for eleven minutes now, running the same numbers through three different models, and every single one ends at the same place. She pushes her glasses up her nose, touches her workstation's haptic interface to pull the temperature projection onto the secondary display. The Pacific sealine temperature data sits beneath it.

9|

The relative scale comparison between the two projections of global mean temperature is wrong. Not wrong like a rounding error. Wrong like the end of the world.

10|

Her lab at NOAA's Climate Monitoring Center in Boulder is quiet at 2:47 AM. The seismic correlation data from USGS has been updating in real time since 01:14. She'd been asleep when the first automated alerts fired. Now she's awake and wishes she weren't.

11|

The Yellowstone caldera has erupted.

12|

Not a hydrothermal event. Not a dome-building episode like the monitoring teams have tracked and dismissed every few years for the past three decades. The magnetometer readings alone told her that within the first four minutes. The pattern matched nothing in the historical record since Instrumental Seismology began. They matched the paleoclimate data from 630,000 years ago. The last supereruption.

13|

She pulls up the ash plume satellite feed. The GOES-18 westward-looking capture shows a dark-gray column punching through the stratosphere at an altitude no model had predicted. Forty kilometers. Forty-two now. It is growing before her eyes.

14|

Elena's hands are shaking. She picks up the encrypted landline, the red one, and dials three digits.

15|

"This is Vasquez, NMCC Boulder. Priority Omega."

16|

The silence on the other end lasts four seconds. She hears a tone and then a dozen voices in the background. Someone has already made the call before her.

17|

---

18|

0430 hours, the Situation Room is full. Elena stands at the podium and no one is sitting down.

19|

She clicks to the third slide — her own hastily reconstructed projection of the eruption cycle, historical mean, and the actual plotted data. The red line of actual observations has already exceeded the 99th percentile of the worst-case model by a factor of two. Then she clicks to the climate model. The aerosol loading curve turns the room so quiet she can hear the air handlers.

20|

"You're going to ask me how bad." Elena's voice is steady, but it cracks at the edges. She's been a scientist for twenty-two years and she has never once said anything more important than what she says next. "I've run three models. They all say the same thing. Five degrees inside eighteen months. Twelve at the upper bound — but I hope I'm wrong about that number."

21|

Someone — she does not see who — sets a coffee cup down hard.

22|

"It will not stop there. The albedo feedback from expanding snow cover will accelerate cooling. New glacial equilibrium within five to eight years. This is not a volcanic winter. This is the onset of a full ice age."

23|

The Secretary-General, Amara Osei, sits at the center of the long table. She has a legal pad in front of her. She has written nothing on it.

24|

"How certain are you?" asks the Chinese delegate.

25|

Elena meets his eyes. "I've been a scientist for twenty-two years. I've never been this certain about anything."

26|

She watches them do the arithmetic. Seven billion people on a planet whose agriculture is calibrated to a very narrow thermal window. A three-degree drop doesn't mean everyone turns on the heat. It means the breadbasket growing seasons cut short by forty days. The Midwest, the Ukraine, the Punjab — gone. Eight billion mouths. Four billion after two years is the actuarial estimate. She does not say this. Someone else has already put it on the shared situation board.

27|

---

28|

At 0800 an emergency UN General Assembly convenes in New York. Nothing prepared anyone for what follows.

29|

Director Alexei Volkov of the International Aerospace Consortium walks to the podium to face one hundred ninety-three delegations. He is sixty-one years old. He has run crewed orbital operations for Roscosmos, ESA, CNSA, NASA, and JAXA combined, sequentially, and landed every one of them. When he speaks, flight directors listen even now, in a stone and glass building on the East River, and he knows it.

30|

"We have a proposal," Volkov says. He does not preamble. "It is called Project Lightship. Its aim is not to save the Earth. The Earth will survive. Its aim is to save us."

31|

He activates the presentation behind him. A rendering of a structure appears on the screen — an ultra-thin membrane four kilometers across, billowing in simulated sunlight, trailing a spine of connected habitat modules like a seed pod behind a flower.

32|

"Laser-sail propulsion. A phased-array laser installation on the lunar surface, fifty gigawatts continuous output, fabricated from in-situ regolith. It will accelerate a fleet of light-sail craft to three percent of the speed of light. Each craft carries a hibernation crew in cryogenic suspension. Nearest viable exoplanet target in the Proxima Centauri system — 4.24 light-years. Transit time is approximately one hundred twenty years."

33|

The room is silent.

34|

"Fifty-eight ships," Volkov continues. " Carrying three hundred and ten souls each. Seventeen thousand nine hundred and eighty people. Enough genetic and cultural diversity to establish viable colonies. The sails are constructed from aluminized graphene laminate. Four kilometers across. Thin — thinner than a soap bubble relative to their span. We have the material science. We have the laser technology. What we do not have is time."

35|

He pauses. The silence is enormous.

36|

"Eighteen months," he says. "That is how long we have before the climate collapse makes large-scale industrial mobilization impossible. Eighteen months to build fifty-eight ships, fabricate the lunar laser array, train the crews, and launch. Can we do it?"

37|

The question hangs. One hundred ninety-three delegations. Several hundred aides and advisors and heads of state.

38|

No one speaks.

39|

Volkov waits. He is good at waiting. He once sat in a Soyuz capsule for eleven hours on the launch pad during a weather hold and did not raise his heart rate above sixty-two.

40|

"We can," he finally says. "The plans existed before the catastrophe — we were already building the first sail sections in 2047. Eight years of pre-study. This is not a desperate improvisation. This is an acceleration of work already in progress. But the timeline is thin and it is physically possible. I will show you the numbers."

41|

He clicks through the slides — the manufacturing plan drawn from every major aerospace and fabrication concern on six continents, the launch cadence, the hibernation protocols adapted from emergency cryopreservation research, the neural maintenance systems.

42|

"And the survival rate for hibernation?" asks the Secretary-General.

43|

"The cryogenic suspension is not speculative. We have maintained mammalian subjects in stasis for up to eleven years with ninety-four percent revival viability. But twelve decades is not eleven years. The aggregate survival probability per individual at the end of the voyage is approximately seventy percent."

44|

Seventy percent. The number settles into the room like ash.

45|

"What happens to the other thirty percent?" someone asks.

46|

Volkov meets the question directly. "They don't wake up."

47|

---

48|

By midnight the vote is tallied. One hundred seventy-one in favor. Twelve abstentions. Ten opposed. Project Lightship is authorized. The largest coordinated engineering effort in human history begins tomorrow.

49|

Elena Vasquez watches the vote tallied on a monitor in her hotel room in Manhattan. She is exhausted. She finds herself wondering for how much longer the electrical grid will sustain this building. Eighteen months.

50|

On her laptop the satellite feed still shows the ash plume. It has wrapped one-third of the way around the equator. The leading edge glows a dull amber at sunset. In a month it will be everywhere. In six months the first frosts will come to the tropics and not leave.

51|

Her phone buzzes. A text from the nursing home in Boulder. Her mother's facility is on emergency generator power. The staff is asking families to check in.

52|

Elena stares at the message. Her mother is seventy-eight years old, three hundred miles away, in a building that will run out of diesel in nine days. She types back: On my way. Then she looks at the launch schedule on her laptop — eighteen months to build the fleet, eighteen months before any ship leaves, eighteen months during which the ash cloud will spread and the power grids will fail and the nursing homes will run out of diesel.

53|

She closes the laptop and switches off the light. The city outside her window is still burning bright — all of Manhattan lit up in defiance of everything, which is the most human response she can imagine, and the one that breaks her heart.

Chapter 2: Chapter 2: The Kovacs Briefing

6|
7|

![](chapter_images/ch02.png)

8|

The call comes at 0630 while James Kovacs is running his sixth mile through Fort Bragg's smoke-stained dawn. His phone vibrates against his thigh with a pattern he has never received before — three pulses, two pulses, three pulses. He stops. He bends over with his hands on his knees and reads the screen: PRIORITY ALPHA REPORT TO BRAGG HQ AMB. NOW.

9|

He has held Priority Alpha clearance for eleven years. He has received the activation signal exactly once, and that was a drill.

10|

He changes direction and runs the remaining two miles to post.

11|

---

12|

The briefing room is on sublevel three of Building 2-3410, behind a door with no placard and three separate biometric checks. James is on time in running gear and a staff duty shirt, which is the best he can do. He has been awake for forty-one hours on four hours of sleep supporting joint Special Operations exercises in the Pacific theater, and then someone has summoned him back across the world on six hours' notice. He smells like a goat and is aware of it when he sees the other occupants.

13|

The room holds eleven people. Nine of them are in suits. Of those nine, three wear the unmistakable look of people who brief four-star generals for a living. A man with the build and stillness of career intelligence sits in the corner and does not make eye contact with anyone.

14|

The tenth person is a colonel from the Air Force Personnel Command whom James recognizes vaguely. The eleventh is Director Alexei Volkov.

15|

James has seen Volkov once, at a joint aerospace operations conference in Houston, three years ago. The room had been full of pilots and engineers. Volkov had spoken for ten minutes about the limits of reentry vehicle design and every person in the room had understood that he was the smartest man present.

Chapter 37: Chapter 37: The Age of Lightships

6|
7|

![](chapter_images/ch37.png)

8|

One hundred and twenty years after the last ship left the Solar System, fifty-eight vessels sail through the dark between stars.

9|

They are spread across a volume of space that would have been unimaginable to the engineers who designed them—a cone of metal and carbon-fiber and frozen human tissue, widening slowly as minute differences in sail angle and ship mass separate them over the decades. The lead ship, Ship 7, is eleven billion kilometers ahead of the trailing Ship 41. Between them, the others drift in a loose formation that no one planned and no one controls, each vessel following the same invisible highway of light, each one riding a beam that has been pushing steadily since before any of the current wake crew was born.

10|

Behind them, Earth is a frozen white memory. The Sun is still visible—it will be for another century yet, a bright star that future generations will learn to call by its proper name rather than the common one. But the Earth itself is invisible to the naked eye, a pale dot lost in the solar glare, and even through the ships' telescopes it appears only as a featureless white sphere, its oceans sealed under kilometers of ice, its atmosphere collapsed into nitrogen snow on the night side. Nothing moves there. Nothing will move there for a very long time.

11|

Ahead of them, Proxima Centauri grows brighter by the decade. It is still a red smudge in the telescopes, still too faint to cast a shadow on the sails, but it is coming. The ships' navigation computers, maintained and recalibrated by a hundred years of wake crews, confirm it daily: deceleration phase will begin in approximately four years. The sail will be reoriented. The same beam that pushed them out will now push against them, slowing their velocity from fourteen kilometers per second to the crawl that will allow orbital insertion around Proxima's single habitable-zone planet. The math is the same. The physics is the same. Only the direction of the push has changed.

12|

The wake crews have rotated seven hundred and twenty times.

13|

Each rotation is six months. Each wake crew member serves seven rotations over the course of the transit, thirty-six months total out of a hundred and twenty years. The rest of the time, they sleep alongside the colonists in identical pods, their dreams running parallel, their bodies maintained by the same systems, their lives measured out in the slow rhythm of wake and hibernation that has become the heartbeat of the fleet.

14|

Seven hundred and twenty rotations. Seven hundred and twenty times, a human being has opened their eyes in a metal tube between the stars and checked the systems and confirmed the sail and counted the green lights on the hibernation bay ceiling. Seven hundred and twenty times, someone has sat in a captain's chair and spoken into a log recorder and said, in one way or another: we are still here. We are still going. The dream is intact.

15|

They have not all been easy rotations.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

cross_profile.description: Opt out of the cross-profile soft guard. Defaults to false. Set true ONLY after explicit user direction to edit another Hermes profile's skills/plugins/cron/memories.

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — bg without notify runs SILENTLY and you have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself. Two legitimate uses:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — silent is correct, there's no exit to notify on.
  (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — MUST set notify_on_complete=true. Without it you'll either forget to poll or sit blocked waiting for the user to surface the result.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — without it, the process runs silently and you'll have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself (easy to forget, leading to silent blindness on long jobs). Two legitimate patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — these stay silent because there's no exit to notify on. (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — these MUST set notify_on_complete=true. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits. Auto-runs syntax checks on .py/.json/.yaml/.toml and other linted languages; only NEW errors introduced by this write are surfaced (pre-existing errors are filtered out).

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

cross_profile.description: Opt out of the cross-profile soft guard. Defaults to false. Set true ONLY after explicit user direction to edit another Hermes profile's skills/plugins/cron/memories — by default these writes are blocked with a warning because they affect a different profile than the one this session is running under.
